utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll start with hearing the testimony of the next witness through videolink. Let's first check whether the videolink is functioning well. At this moment, Madam Registrar, at the other side of the videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We hear you; we see you. Do you hear us? Do you see us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. We can hear you; we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the videolink room. I do understand that it would be a witness who testifies without protective measures and that it would Mr. Dragan Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar at the videolink location, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. And could you also tell us who, apart from you, are present in the videolink room. Madam Registrar will tell us in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar at the videolink location, could you tell us who are in the room with you at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, apart from myself, there is the witness and ICTY ITSS technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness, Mr. Vujcic. Mr. Vujcic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujcic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujcic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll see him soon on your screen. Mr. Lukic is counsel for the -- for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us for the record slowly your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I am Dragan Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll make a brief pause before I put my questions to you because I'm waiting for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you given a statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see on our screens 1D05895.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujcic, can you see it on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, "Witness Statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this page before you, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see the signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: It's my signature again, Dragan Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you had an opportunity to review this statement? Does it reflect accurately what you've said to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've reviewed it and it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it truthful?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you again today the same questions, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers as the first time. That's -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would now like to tender the statement of Mr. Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D5895 receives Exhibit Number D1359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just read the short statement of Mr. Vujcic and I will not have any questions for our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujcic, I will now read a short version of your statement for the public to know its contents. [In English] I didn't provide copies to the booths. We had some problems with the printer this morning, so I just have one copy of it that I printed yesterday. I'll read slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read slowly, that will certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness, Dragan Vujcic, was trained during his regular military service in the JNA to carry out engineering tasks, and he was in the village where he was born in Prijedor municipality when the war broke out. He received his mobilisation papers there on 16th of September, 1991, and he was assigned to the engineering battalion of what was then the 343rd Motorised Brigade of the JNA. He speaks about the structure of his engineering battalion, the number of personnel, manning and equipment levels, and the ethnic structure of the unit. He also describes the war history of his unit and his combat dispositions and asserts that his unit and its equipment were deployed in the Gradacac front, apart from a logistics unit, quartered in the village of Orlovaca in the Prijedor sector whose task was to repair damaged machinery. He says that his unit never received any orders relating to the Tomasica mine and nor were its machines used to bury bodies in Tomasica. Personnel from his unit did not have any part in these burials. In this context, he says that any suggestion that he was ever in Tomasica would not be correct because the first time he heard of Tomasica was through the media when the bodies were being excavated. So that is short summary statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujcic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. D'Ascoli. Ms. D'Ascoli will soon appear on your screen. Ms. D'Ascoli is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will have some questions for you this morning, although I won't keep you for long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not only have questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we have some music as well apparently - not my preferred music, but that doesn't matter. Music is over now again. Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Vujcic, I was saying I will have some questions for this morning. So, sir, you mentioned in paragraph 5 of your statement, now admitted as D1359, that you were mobilised into the 343rd Motorised Brigade of the JNA on 16 September 1991. At that time your brigade commander was Vladimir Arsic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That brigade became the 43rd Motorised Brigade of the VRS on 19 May 1992, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And Colonel Arsic remained commander; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And Captain Dragan Gajic remained your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I have D866 on the screen, please, and I would ask that the first page in both languages be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, while the document is appearing on the screens, you mentioned in paragraph 7 of your statement that you were deployed back to Prijedor in May 1992 before leaving again to the front. Now the document is on the screen. This is a 5th Corps daily combat report to the 2nd Military District dated 3 May 1992. I will direct your attention to point 2, the second paragraph of the document on the screen, and you have -- it's the same in the B/C/S, yes. Now, point 2, second paragraph, and I will read: "In the course of 2 and 3 May, one 105-millimetre Howitzer battery and one anti-armour artillery battery of the 343rd Motorised Brigade were relocated to the Prijedor area in order to strengthen the units in the wider Prijedor-Ljubija-Kozarac area." You have seen that, sir, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that these units were relocated to Prijedor in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that because we stayed on in the Croatian battle-field to hand over the minefields to the Nepalese Battalion of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to that. So in paragraph 7 of your statement you say that you and the engineers of your battalion returned to Prijedor from the Croatian front in May 1992. You then state that after a short rest period in Prijedor, you were sent to the Gradacac front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, Gradacac is about 190 kilometres away from Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you remember when you went to Gradacac after a period of rest in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: It was a short rest, some five days. We mainly stayed in the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks in Prijedor. We parked our motor vehicles, and after five days we left for the front line in Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you mean that it was the same month, May 1992, or was it later, if you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And your deployment there was part of the corridor operation? I mean your deployment to Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we have P3841 to the screen, please. And if we can turn to page 5 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, the document that will be appearing on the screen is an interview with Radmilo Zeljaja published in the Kozarski Vjesnik in 1994. Now in 1992 Zeljaja was the deputy commander of your brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, could you direct us where the B/C/S we can find this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. In the B/C/S it is the fourth column. The part that I'm going to refer to starts at the very bottom where -- and then it continues on -- unfortunately, it continues on page 1 and the last column because it's an article, so it reads in columns. So it will be probably -- we will have to ask the Court Officer to go back and forth. But if I start reading from -- in the B/C/S, it's page 2 at the very bottom of the fourth column, while in English we can follow at page 5 -- yeah. So the English and this is the part that starts with Radmilo Zeljaja being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I will read the part that I will be referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And at some point in the B/C/S we have to -- after the first line, we have to move to page 1, the beginning of the fifth column.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So maybe, sir, I will ask you to start reading and then I will give you time to catch up. You can also listen to the translation, of course. So I quote -- Zeljaja here is asked about the deployment of the 43rd Brigade units to the corridor and he says: "Yes, we were given the task to leave and help the forces to break the corridor of life. At that time, we mobilised the 2nd Battalion" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we switch now.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, please move in B/C/S to page 1, the beginning of the fifth column. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: "At that time we mobilised the 2nd Battalion of Major Slijepcevic reinforced it with artillery, armoured, and other units, and set off across Trebava and Doboj to accomplish the task." Could you follow that, sir? Did you read that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree that this is the deployment of the 43rd Brigade units to the corridor that resulted in you and your unit going to Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, continuing with the quote, Zeljaja says: "We arrived at the appropriate region before Saint Vitus Day and we were gradually preparing to be introduced into the battle." Sir, Saint Vitus Day is the 28th of June; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So it was, in fact, late June 1992 when those 43rd Brigade units that went to the corridor were deployed there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't see that everybody should read the same way. It says "just before Vidov Dan they were," that's what it says here, "before Vidov Dan," that doesn't say when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A matter which you can raise in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you -- sir, until when did you stay to the Gradacac front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: We stayed until 1995, from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. I move to the different area. Sir, in your statement, paragraph 9, now D1359, you say that the chief engineer was Reserve Captain Slobodan Skoric. He was the chief engineer of your brigade, of the 43rd Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief of the engineering battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: And the commander was Dragan Gajic. I was man number three, Gajic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. What was the role of the chief engineer of the 43rd?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Well, the chief engineer was in contact with the brigade command. Commands came through him to Commander Gajic; and I, together with the troops, dealt with the digging of trenches, construction of roads, supplies to the brigade with heating, fuel, water, et cetera. We did everything the brigade asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And what were your dealings with him, with the chief engineer, with Captain Slobodan Skoric? How often would you see him and so on? That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Well, he spent more time at the brigade command than together with us. Gajic and I were with the troops and we carried out the works, the assignments, we received from the brigade command -- I mean engineering works, any that were needed, placing minefields, barriers, digging trenches, supplying --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That's clear, sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: -- et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you know Slobodan Skoric from Prijedor in 1991, before you were both mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm receiving French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: However much I like the French language, it should not be on the English channel. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skoric was the chief of engineers even before the war broke out in 1991. That was an engineering company then at that time. He was always at the head of the engineering units. He was the best person for that in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we have P7385 on the screen, please. And if we go to page 5 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, sir, you knew what his job was before being mobilised, you said chief engineer, head of the engineer units. Do you know where he was working?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Skoric worked at the Ljubija mine as a technical officer. I think he was in charge of construction.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. We see on this page -- this is, sir, a report from the -- on the work of the company, of the Ljubija mine company, doing war operations in 1992. And on this page we see a list of workers of the company that were mobilised into the VRS. And in fact, I want to direct your attention to the middle of the page where we read: "Mining sector, head Slobodan Skoric." So as you said, you were aware that he was the head of the mining sector at the RZR Ljubija; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now as head of the mining sector Ljubija, he would have known well the resources, the machines available, at the mine company, et cetera; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. For the most part, he was the mine's technical director.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you yourself knew the RZR Ljubija mine company in Prijedor; right? Were you aware and did you know the type of resources and machines that the company had at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, superficially. I know that they had the mining equipment. They had bulldozers, dumpers, excavators, trucks. Yes, they had all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's say the 43rd Brigade needed to dig a trench or build a road in Prijedor and your unit and its equipment was at the front - for example, as you said, at the Gradacac front - the brigade would use mobilised resources from Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: We had military vehicles and military machinery that went with us to the Gradacac front.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but can you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: And, yes, we used them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So my question was: If you -- your units and your machines were away at the front and the 43rd Brigade or other units in Prijedor needed to dig a trench, or build a road, something that would have been done by your unit and by the machines of your units, now would they use mobilised resources from Prijedor when your unit was away, was not there in Prijedor? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Base for the question: Which other brigade would be on the Prijedor area, if he knows whether ever another brigade would be in Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not an objection, as a matter of fact. It is a question which you'd like to put to the witness which you of course can put --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the basis for the question -- there is no base for this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you think there isn't, then that's certainly is a matter which can you raise in re-examination. But since Ms. D'Ascoli is now aware of your concerns and if she puts the question to the witness perhaps again, she may even take that into account. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object, foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, the question was -- I wasn't referring to the unit of the witness. I think there is a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said if other -- "brigade."

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, I didn't say "brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, first of all, we still behave civilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try not to interrupt each other. Perhaps you read the question again. There may be a translation issue, you never know. I don't know whether Mr. Lukic listened in English or not. Would you please put the question to the witness again, Ms. D'Ascoli, and if there's any objection, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's line -- it's page 13, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, a second ago I said let's not -- let's invite - and that what's I did - Ms. D'Ascoli to again put the question, either exactly in the same words or in slightly different words, to the witness. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli, and once you have put the question to the witness before he starts answering, Mr. Lukic certainly will have a moment to jump up if he thinks that that's what he should do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I will repeat my question. So let's say the 43rd Brigade needed to dig a trench or build a road in Prijedor, and your unit - meaning the engineer battalion of the 43rd - with its equipment was elsewhere, was at the front, was at the Gradacac front. Now the brigade, and I mean other units of the brigade, would use mobilised resources from Prijedor? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: That is something that I don't know. In my area of work we had all the military vehicles in the field, excavators, machinery for road construction, bulldozers, trucks. All of those machines mostly were with us at the Gradacac front.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I think you've answered in the very beginning by saying that you don't know, and then you explained something I think you said before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now I think we still have P7385 on our screen. Can we please move to page 7 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, there is evidence in this case that the 43rd Brigade mobilised resources from the Ljubija mine company. Besides the document that is now on the screen, I can refer to P7319 or P7423. Were you aware of such mobilisation of resources from the RZR Ljubija to the 43rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. It was mobilised right at the beginning, once we set off there and we also had the FAP trucks with us there, military vehicles, these 110s, 150s, and we had bulldozers. All of that was at the Gradacac front for the main part. As far as I know, all of that was there and that was where we set up roads, provided the entire brigade with timber and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, you just described -- yes, what there is in the statement and the fact that you, with the equipment of your battalion, were away from Prijedor. Now, can I direct your attention to the list of motor vehicles, machines, such as graders, excavators, loaders, that we see on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In the English, it is split between page 7 and the following page, but the first one will suffice for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, sir, you see in the column War Unit the code 4777 which is the code for the 43rd Brigade of the VRS, your brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And then we see also the code 8316 which was the one for the 5th Kozara Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Then we see two other codes, 6817, 5456. These were VRS brigades not based in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: That was all out in the field mostly at the Gradacac front and Brcko, mostly along those two axes, the Prijedor 5th Kozara and the 43rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Were you referring to the code 6817 and 5456 or to all of the codes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about all of the codes, some were in the 5th Kozara Brigade and some in the 43rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. So this is a report on the war operations of the mine in the course of 1992. So were you aware that the equipment of the Ljubija mine company was used by these VRS units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was and it was out there in the field, in Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So now can we have P7424.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, this is a handwritten log, again from the RZR Ljubija, which provides an overview of the allocated and used quantities of fuel for the VRS for the period January 1992 to May 1993. Now, if you look at, for example, entries number 8 or 13 to 19, these are for the dates June to July 1992. We see references to a D8L, a bulldozer; G16, a grader -- okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. This was road construction in Gradacac. We were tunnelling through a hill using a bulldozer that arrived later from Prijedor. This was mainly happening on the Gradacac front.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at the -- for example, entry -- yes, number 19 or number 13 as well as number 15, you see the mention of Luke, Luke dump site. Now, were you aware that this Luke site is on RZR Ljubija property?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Are you aware that this site is on the RZR Ljubija property?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I didn't know any of that. All I know is that the machine came up there to Gradacac, that's the dozer, the bulldozer, and we were constructing roads, detours leading to Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. We have seen that there were a number of bulldozers from the list. Now you said you don't -- you didn't know that this site was on RZR Ljubija property. You said you had never been present in Tomasica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was never up there, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, in particular, you were not there between June or July 1992 and -- well, you said you were at the front until 1995. So you had no idea what was going on at Tomasica or on the RZR Ljubija mine property during that period; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything until a while back when the exhumations were carried out. I didn't even know about the camp. I spent most of the time at the front. My commander and the chief spent more time at the command and in Prijedor, and they would come and go there. So I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: They probably know more than I do. I was at the front. I was this with the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I've one question seeking clarification. Looking at this list and looking at the -- what is read to you, such as I think it was D8L-4/51, is that a type of equipment or is that a single piece of equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you because when it was read to you, you said: This was road construction in Gradacac. Now, how would you know -- if these are not individual pieces of equipment, how would you know whether this was a reference to a similar piece of equipment which was not in Gradacac? I mean, how are you able to link this description to the equipment that was in Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that we had rented this more powerful machine, this bulldozer, in order to work on an alternate route, on a detour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you used such a machine - that's your recollection - but do you know whether another machine of the same type was used elsewhere, that is, in another location than Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in Prijedor at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Now, do you have any explanation as to the mentioning of Luke in some of these -- could you -- would you please wait until I have finished my question. Do you have any explanation as to why the word "Luke" appears in this list in the same line with the equipment D8L/51 or other equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have an explanation because I'm not familiar with that abbreviation. I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what Luke means or what ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Yes, I don't know what these numbers mean either. It's an abbreviation of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the numbers D8L/51, you don't know what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what that stands for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it refresh your memory if it was an abbreviation for a specific type of equipment, type of machinery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that that's an abbreviation for some kind of machinery. I mean, really, I don't know what it stands for. I see lower down that there is another mention of that underneath also, another 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Just a second. I'll read the last answers. Just a second. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, sir, do you agree that you don't have any basis to say -- out of the resources and machines mobilised from the RZR Ljubija, you don't have any basis to say which ones and how many stayed in Prijedor on RZR Ljubija mine property and which ones, and how many, were sent - as you claim - to the Gradacac front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what was done in Prijedor. This is something that the people in the brigade command probably know, because all the orders came from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And is there any reason for which you can exclude that parts of the VRS that had stayed in Prijedor could have been involved in the burial of bodies at Tomasica with resources, machines, mobilised from the RZR Ljubija? Is there any reason for which you can exclude that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I'm not aware of any of that, because I was out in the field continuously. I was in Gradacac and in -- and I don't know what was going on in Prijedor. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I don't have further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope we'll -- if we can continue for next five to ten minutes, maybe we could finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is -- if that would be agreeable to Mr. Mladic as well, then we could finish the videolink in five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We -- if I could continue, we are -- I need this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same document that is in front of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- which is P7424.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujcic, we can see here under number 2 for the 28th of May that it states: "D8/50. Road to Luke ..." Let me ask you: Do you know how often, for example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina there would be an area named Luke? Is that a common name for some region, or is that something specific for Prijedor? Did you come across places or areas with the same name in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it means, "road to Luke," Luka ... I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In late May 1992, were you constructing some roads in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: No. We went directly to Gradacac in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now: Did any other unit from the 43rd Brigade have the ability to do mining, road construction, laying mines? Could the infantry do that or the communications unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Well, those who were in Prijedor would probably have been able to do that. I know that my engineering unit didn't do any of that because we had our hands full at Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any part of your engineering unit that stayed in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have those workmen in Prijedor who repaired machines when they broke down. There was perhaps one squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've just found out - Mr. Ivetic, my colleague, is showing me - training ground Luke, Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were in Gradacac, did you hear about a part of Gradacac called Luke?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: There are many Lukes there, because it's mostly high ground and Luke is low ground. So when you construct a road, you go to the low ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when Mr. Ivetic whispered in your ear, Luke training ground, did he tell you that you if you would use that in a question that it would be highly leading and that that's what you're supposed not to do, or didn't he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- no, Mr. Lukic, it's leading. What you could have asked was: Do you know of any location close to Gradacac known by the name Luke or Luka? That's phrasing the question rather than to introduce already that there must be a place where there's a training ground. And let's leave it to that. Let's move on. The question has been put. The question has been answered. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But also the witness explained actually what kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes, the witness gave an answer which did not follow your lead. That doesn't make the question any less leading. And not any less inappropriate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on our screens P3841, please. [Interpretation] In the B/C/S, we need page 2; in English, page 5. The fourth column, that's where we began. [In English] Then we move to the next -- top of the next paragraph, 5 in B/C/S, please, page 2. Page 2. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was put to you that Saint Vitus Day was 28th June 1992. When did you set off from Prijedor to the corridor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: To the corridor? We set off by bus from the barracks. We went by bus from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But do you remember when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember now when. Usually you set off in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I mean the date. Did you set out on the 28th of June, 1992, when the corridor was opened up, or before that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Later. We set out later. Because we returned later from the Croatian theatre of war. Because, first, we had to hand over the minefields to the Nepalese battalion of the UNPROFOR. So we arrived late at the corridor. I think a month later, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the corridor was opened up. Towards the end of July or in August?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. May, June, July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification. Sir, when you say you arrived there later, you arrived later than what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, later than our brigade. After the infantry battalions left. Because we stayed on at the Croatian theatre of war to turn over the minefields and the rest to the Nepalese battalion of the UNPROFOR. I can't remember exactly how long after the departure of the brigade with the infantry battalions. But they went first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to remember whether you went there on or before the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around that time, yes. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't place it whether it was before the 28th or after the 28th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we could link it to an event. Did you arrive before the corridor was opened up, or did you arrive when the corridor had already been opened up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: The corridor had already been opened up. That's when we departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujcic. We have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUJCIC
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further. Mr. Vujcic, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the videolink location and for answering all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. Therefore, again, thank you. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you too. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar at the videolink location, we can conclude the videolink now and we'll continue here in The Hague. Thank you for your assistance. We take a break, and we'll resume --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Lukic, I was informed -- the Chamber was informed that there was a matter you'd like to raise and perhaps we should do that in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, I had one or two on my list as well, but let's see whether you have the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, I see that we have the completely new set of our learned friends from the opposite side. But we would ask the Prosecution if we can stipulate that there is a Luke area in Gradacac municipality; and if we cannot stipulate that, since that issue arose in this cross-examination, we would like to upload two documents with this site in Gradacac area, and one of them even contains the exact co-ordinates for that place. That's one matter. And the other matter is I forget yesterday to propose again to have D00557 MFI'd until we propose the portions of the document. We do not intend to -- we do not intend to offer the whole document into evidence but we would make a selection and - in communication with our learned friends from the opposite if they want to include anything from that book or pamphlet - then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean "The Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Two matters. First, Luke -- something was unclear to me, Mr. Lukic. When you introduced that as a training site, was there -- was that in evidence anywhere up till this moment or did it spontaneously come up and being something -- a new element hidden in your question? I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you because Luke you can find in any municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, that's not my question. My question was: Whether anywhere in the evidence we find a reference to Luke as a training site close to Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, so apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I'll check, maybe I can check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you introduce it in a question without knowing --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not likely, I can tell you, but I cannot exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's one. Then stipulation about a place called Luke near Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, any additional information that counsel would have regarding information on the record would assist. Other than that, I will speak to my colleagues and get back to the Chamber in terms of the particular question concerning the stipulation today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's one. Then the second issue was about - and let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the selection from "The Islamic Declaration."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has considered its position with respect to this, and I do understand that the Chamber has inquired about the Defence submissions on multiple occasions about it. We further considered it and discussed it with the Defence, and we indicated that it may be best actually to have the complete document in evidence. And we did -- I was informed subsequent to my last time up about this document, that there had been discussions to actually allow the whole document into evidence. So I appreciate Mr. Lukic's patience with this, but that would be our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, of course, the Chamber finds itself in a bit of an odd position because we are blamed for opposing admission of "The Islamic Declaration," which we strongly rejected yesterday. At the same time, if you give us a document of hundred pages with quite a bit of substance and then say: You, Chamber, do whatever you want to do with it, that's of course another matter because Chamber and the Chamber staff will start reading it, will start analysing it, even if it's not related to -- major portions are not related to any questions put to a witness. And it seems that the parties now and then forget that if you dump something into evidence, that this Chamber takes evidence seriously, that is, that we have to look at it. And that's the one and only reason perhaps why we were a bit reluctant to immediately admit it into evidence in its entirety, and not in any way what was suggested by the Defence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add one word about translation. There is no translation. We have an English version, a different publication with many differences with respect to the B/C/S original. That -- in fact two originals, and therefore before we discuss the matter and decide on it, we should know if it is really necessary to ask CLSS to produce a new translation of the entire book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did it already, Your Honour, we sent it to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. If it's all of it now, we'll have to have your help on that issue because CLSS refuses to translate books or documents of that size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you do that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Recently, when the problem arose, that the translation is not correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then it's yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course, this Chamber is always willing to assist the parties in getting the translations they need. I think that's constant approach we've taken. At the same time, I think that on the basis of the English version that exists, that the parties would be encouraged to see if we really need all of it, again for the reasons -- even if Prosecution would not oppose it and it may be clear that strong positions -- apparently that's at least what -- that's my first impression not having analysed it, strong positions as to an Islamic state and religion and statehood are expressed there, I can see the relevance, but I don't know whether that's everywhere, whether it's all relevant. And before you, I would say, condemn us to have to read it all where there was no reason to introduce it through witnesses, all of it, you get the Chamber's support, but you first seriously should discuss with the Prosecution whether we need it all because ten pages of translation takes a lot of time and resources. Again, if you agree on the matter, if you also make it clear that it is relevant, that we should see it all, then you get our full support; but you should first do that job together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour the position of Defence is not that we need the whole, but we want to accommodate the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If they want the whole thing, then it's fine with the Defence; otherwise, we would rather have just portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the Prosecution should make clear why they want more than the Defence wants, where it seems to me at least that "The Islamic Declaration" is a -- something the Defence wants to rely upon in its defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we have some portions -- because some portions are, I think, not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Weber, would you please -- apart from saying let's dump it as a whole, could you please make a serious effort to -- for contextualisation to select any portions in addition what the Defence wants to have in?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll hear from you -- well, let's say, not later than Monday because -- yes? So that -- and if CLSS is starting to translate -- perhaps they could start with the portions --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was corrected, Your Honour. I didn't transfer the message correctly. Our Case Manager just informed us that he is still waiting which parts he should send, so it's not sent yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. But awaiting your -- your agreement on what portions should be sent for translation, I think you want to add something to what is already submitted by the Defence. So therefore, you could also say, To start with, not the whole book but these and these portions which were dealt with in court or these and these pages we have selected, and then we don't face further delays.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask to be excused. I'll continue working on that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, before you leave the courtroom, any other matter you would like to raise? If not, I would have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour. I will wait until you deliberate yours and then I will try to ask you to excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- we expected to receive further in information about ongoing conversations about the Dunjic report the beginning of this week. We're now halfway the week, so the Chamber would like to receive an update.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. McCloskey is more informed about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- so if I could defer to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We have made our view clear, that we're fine with the Dunjic's report and that Mr. Stankovic relying on Dunjic's report and that our preference is not a whole new Stankovic report and the ball is now in their court on that point. So we were hoping to hear from them today as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any thoughts developed on how to proceed? But before you answer that, let me try to understand you, Mr. McCloskey. The Dunjic report has not yet been tendered. It's just -- notice has been given. So your suggestion would be that it would be tendered, that it would be admitted, and that Mr. Stankovic would answer any questions the Prosecution would have in relation to the Dunjic report. And of course, he's not the author of that report, so -- and that is all expertise because Mr. Stankovic would appear as an expert but not on his on expert report. I can imagine that under those circumstances that it would be appropriate that Mr. Stankovic writes a very, very, very short expert report, which is that he has read Mr. Dunjic's report and that he agrees with it or that he has no comments on it from his own expertise, or that he says, Well, page 15, that and that conclusion, I would not adopt that. Or -- well, to -- to introduce Mr. Stankovic as expert because, of course, we can't call Mr. Dunjic as expert. At the same time, Mr. Stankovic hasn't produced that report, and I take it that you would still would like to have an opportunity to put questions to an expert about Mr. Dunjic, his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I was thinking the same thing. Anything brief and to the point even going through and making comments on individual parts of Dr. Dunjic's report is perfectly fine. In addition, what I had mentioned to the Defence is Dr. Dunjic testified at length in the Karadzic case based on a report that is very similar to his Mladic report. And as far as I'm concerned, his testimony from Karadzic could come in, which is fully cross-examined, and avoid the entire problem. I understand they want a live witness and so that's what we are trying to work out, that the live witness come, defend the report, defend his own views of the report, gets cross-examined, and we get this done in a -- hopefully before the end of January is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was exploring what you had on your mind because the technicalities involved require some further thoughts about what is in evidence, who testifies about what, own report, someone else's report, what's the basis for that, does he appear as a witness or as an expert witness. These are technical matters which should be -- thoroughly be considered before we -- before the parties suggest a final solution. Mr. Lukic, apart from these technicalities, the main issue, that is, we have a report of which is given notice to the Chamber and to the Prosecution, it's not tendered yet. It is -- what are your plans?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our plan is to bring Mr. Stankovic as soon as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but he has to tell us when. I cannot promise you the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you do not intend to ask Mr. Stankovic to write a whole new report. We would work --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The starting point --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not your intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he might need to do some work on the report. He has to go through the report, to check, to see if he accepts all the parts or if he can talk about all the parts, so still there is some time required for him to go through the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's not the intention to have a new report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to familiarise -- that Mr. Stankovic familiarises himself with the content of the report, that's understood. And that, of course, takes far less time than to produce a report, but it certainly will take some time. Second, the transcript of the cross-examination of Mr. Dunjic in Karadzic case, is there any -- any objection to -- because I take it that that's where Mr. Dunjic explained and answered further questions in relation to a report which is, to some extent, similar - if I understand you well - to the report produced in the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I cannot give you the answer now. You know that we objected to the use of cross-examination from another case, as it was the proposal at the beginning of the Defence case. So now we would have to depart to that basic standpoint of the Defence, but of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is -- of course the situation is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- yeah, exactly. I -- the situation is completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then -- apparently there is no disagreement that no full new report should be drafted and that Mr. Stankovic would familiarize himself and would check whether he would agree. Then could you further discuss with Prosecution and urgently how to deal with the cross-examination in the Karadzic case because that is then an open issue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, a solution in which the Dunjic report would admit into evidence without Mr. Stankovic further explaining, without -- without relying on the cross-examination of Mr. Dunjic in the Karadzic case, would that be acceptable for you? So that's just a report in and that's it, 94 bis (C) -- no you don't ask for cross-examination. Of course, you couldn't ask for cross-examination but no -- nothing to replace that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My first thought is I'm very, very tempted if I thought the Defence was considering that. That is not something that I had as an option, but I would, of course, discuss that with Mr. Tieger but I am very tempted to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to have it admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have it admitted and we'll argue it in the briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no Mr. Stankovic, no cross-examination in the Karadzic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a very simple and basic thing which I am very tempted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- I need to think about it with Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not what you offered a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, because I didn't think they would go for that. I'm looking for a creative solution. I think that may be an excellent solution, but they wanted a witness is what I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, now we have various options, either with Mr. Stankovic who would then have to prepare a while and then would you have to consider how to present him as an expert witness or as a witness -- and most likely as an expert witness. The other option - or in combination with that first one - would be the introduction of the Karadzic cross-examination or perhaps some of the examination-in-chief as well from Mr. Dunjic. And the third option still considered by the Prosecution, although not yet having decided because they didn't thought you would accept that, that is just to have the expert report in and then leave it to argument later. I'm not asking a final decision now, but just to say: No Stankovic, no cross-examination, we have the report and we'll argue on the basis of that report, and then we'll find out what the merits of the report and what the evidentiary value of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will have in mind the third option as well, Your Honour, but I don't have the answer at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay. That's fine. Could we hear not any later than by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Friday we're not sitting. Monday, not close of business, but start of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we -- sometime is a bit difficult to reach Professor Stankovic, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you make up your mind that you don't need him, then you don't need to reach him either. So on that option --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The third option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The third option, you don't need him. So you can discuss that or think about it, but we would like to hear from you anyhow Monday morning and -- and Mr. Mladic can consult at low volume. I think we have sufficiently discussed the matter at this moment. Let's move on and let's invite the witness to re-enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one point. Mr. Lukic, in fact to make a decision on all three options, you don't need Mr. Stankovic. You'd make the decision and then you tell Mr. Stankovic what you have decided. If you need him, you tell him you need him; if you don't, you tell him: We don't need you any longer on the Dunjic case. So you really don't need Mr. Stankovic to make up your mind. It's your course of action that you must decide on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but if we decide that we need him still, then we have to work with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course, you have got to work with him, but you can give us the decision and then carry on to work with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could address a housekeeping matter while the witness is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 41747, Exhibit P07668 was marked for identification pending a revised translation of the list of names. The revised translation has been uploaded into e-court under document ID 0649-2932-1-ET.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution kindly requests that the Court Officer be asked to replace the current translation with the revised version and the document be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we finalise this right away. Madam Registrar, the translation attached to Exhibit P07668 should be replaced by the newly uploaded revised translation of that list of names, then including ranks, I take it, identified as a document under doc ID 0649-2932-1-ET and you are accordingly instructed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The number should be corrected. It should be 2932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I misread, then -- well, that's hereby clear. It wasn't admitted yet, so P07668 is hereby admitted. Witness, we'll continue. That's to say, that Mr. Weber will continue his cross-examination. I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33511. At the outset here, I'm going to kindly ask the Court Officer to also hand a hard copy of this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday when we were discussing paragraph 4.220 of your report and the Wikipedia page, the Trial Chamber inquired about your cited source in footnote 464, the Slobodna Dalmacija interview of Emin Garaplija. This interview is now on the screen before us and a hard copy has been provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 4 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During this interview, there is only one question and answer that appears to relate to the subject of the paragraph in your report. The interviewer asks: "Who murdered the young couple, a Muslim woman and a Serb man, on one bridge in Sarajevo, on the line of separation? That crime outraged the whole world and Serbs were blamed for it." He then, Garaplija, answered: "That is not true. This was perfidious propaganda of the people who gave orders to Seve. Herenda was specific in connection with that crime in his statement and stated that the couple had been murdered by Dragan Bozic from a sniper rifle. Herenda even described the spot from which Bozic killed them." Here, in this article, there are no references to the names of the couple Admira and Bosko; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps they're not mentioned in the article itself, but just looking at it briefly, the gist is the same in the article. Primarily that means that it's what I insisted on, and that was that the fire came from members of the Seve units and this is not something that's in dispute on the basis of this text either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please focus on my questions because my question specifically pertains to the text that appears in the article. There is no discussion of how Bosko was shot first and then Admira was wounded and died ten minutes later; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view and from the point of view of a military expertise, that is not something that was really crucial and I didn't put any time into that. What was important to me was the media aspect of it, the misuse of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please answer my question. That text is not -- there's no discussion of that in that text in that article; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, are we sure we have the right B/C/S page on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Right under the title, towards the top third of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sequence I read a few sources about the sequence, this text, I read articles from the press, I read books, but mostly I was dealing with the untruthfulness of the whole incident. I did not deal with who fired first and what the sequence was and exactly how it happened. What was important to me was that the crime was ascribed to the Serb side, whereas it was actually carried out by members of the Seve units; that was what I was focussing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think you still have answered my question, but I'll give you one more chance. There's no mention of UN forces or how the bodies were buried in the Lav cemetery in 1996, according to the wishes of Admira's parents, in the article; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Herenda's statement is referred to here that -- he is quoted here as a member, "I fired them when they fell ..." and so on and so forth. And then on the second page, paragraphs 3 to 6. So now I couldn't -- I cannot remember all the different six to ten sources that I used in my report. It's a bit difficult now to recall exactly which sentence came from which source. I was really interested in the essence of the case, and I spoke about that a little bit earlier. I did not deal with the killing on the Vrbanija bridge, but I was dealing with making value judgements about this particular event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've repeated that now many times; that's clear. Your answer started with a "yes," which was an answer to the question. Referring to the many, many sources, of which only one is found in the footnote, was Wikipedia one of the sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the sources that was consulted, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the language used very much similar; is that coincidence or is that ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on a number of sources, if that is the formulation that was the closest reflection of the actual incident, then it's possible that it was taken as the basis for the actual quote itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the B/C/S version on the screen of 1D5358, and if we could go to page 177 of the B/C/S. And next to it, if we could please have the -- bring back up the B/C/S version of 65 ter 33486. And if we could please focus on paragraph 4.220 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, here we have again your report and also the part of the Wikipedia page. In the highlighted part, we see the names of the couple are mentioned, just like in your report; an explanation of how Bosko was shot first and then Admira was wounded ten minutes later; the reference to the UN forces and how the bodies were buried in the Lav cemetery in 1996. The text is almost identical to your report with the minor modification that was made yesterday. This part of your report comes from Wikipedia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just Wikipedia. This same conclusion was published in a series of articles, both in the Serbian and the Bosniak press, and the essence is not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the only source that you cite for this text or even related to this text in your paragraph is the article that you have before you. This text appears nowhere in that article; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formulation doesn't appear, but the essence does. I don't see that it's of dispute if you find out the essence from a number of sources and then cite one source. For one passage, you cannot cite four or five sources that were consulted, because in that case the expert report would not have 600 footnotes but would have thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the article that you contain -- that you have in front of you, which is your one source, does not contain the information that you have in this paragraph; correct? It may refer to the same event, but it definitely does not contain the same details that you describe in your report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data is not linked to the names or this part that has to do with the reburial in the Lav cemetery in Sarajevo, but these are facts that are beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ters 33486 and 33511 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33486 receives Exhibit Number P7670. 65 ter number 33511 receives Exhibit Number P7671, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7670 and P7671 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any other direct lifts from Wikipedia in your report that you have not cited to?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are internal links, for example, there are key events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know if it's a matter of translation, but I neither heard in the B/C/S nor in the English the formulation that Mr. Weber has suggested as to Wikipedia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then -- could you please repeat your question, Mr. Weber, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any other portions of your report where you directly lift language from Wikipedia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without citing to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Without citing to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are many parts where I consulted Wikipedia, but not literally but just as one of the sources. It was not cited as a source, though, but other sources were cited that spoke about the same event or the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But part of the question was that you would have lifted languages, that is, means - if I understand you well, Mr. Weber - that you used completely or to a very large extent the text, the language, used on the Wikipedia page without citing it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot really remember this completely now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to review the paragraphs from the Radinovic reports and compare them to your report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used the afternoon to carry out this task in detail, and I can tell you what my analysis showed --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you very much for doing that. There were paragraphs that were listed on that sheet that contained substantially similar text to those in the Radinovic reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just state the conclusions of the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if could you answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could first answer the question, Witness, and then you'll be given an opportunity to briefly state the conclusions of your analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of the 54 paragraphs given in the text, 35 were paraphrased ranging from 10 to 90 per cent. On average, we're talking about 65 per cent. As for 16 paragraphs, there are indirect quotes and they would be given in the next paragraph or would be covering two pages. There are quotes, and I can say what they are about. Three quotes were dropped from the paragraphs. They do exist. Out of the 54 paragraphs, there are quotes for three paragraphs. And if you need more details about the citations, I can provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just if we could ask -- if I could ask a couple of question [sic]. In the paragraphs in your report that were listed, there were no citations to General Radinovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is cited in these 19 paragraphs that I mentioned a moment ago, whereas in the 35 paragraphs that are paraphrased and relate to facts - and I can tell you what the nature of the concepts is, it's geographic concepts and the structure of forces and such things - the same thing is expressed in a different way in the percentage that I have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I see that you probably went through that quite carefully. Did you mark the individual paragraphs that you -- the 35 that you agree with and the ones that you feel that you do attribute to Mr. Radinovic or do not have a substantial overlap, did you mark those?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every one is marked either as paraphrased or expressed differently. Sixteen citations have already been given for the said paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If it's okay with you and with the Chamber - I don't want to belabour going through all 50 examples - but if we could see that list, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
