utterances.text: And, Your Honours, while the review might answer this for us, but I note that two different numbers have appeared in the translation for the paragraphs with citations, both 16 and 19, although 16 has been used twice. So I don't know which is the correct number, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it be shown to the Defence as well. I don't know whether this document would greatly assist you, Mr. Weber, but just have a look at it. Another way of dealing with the matter would be to ask the witness to write down the numbers of the paragraphs of the category of the 19 or 16, but perhaps you have a look at it during the next break and then we'll see how we can perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was being hopeful that the list would illuminate that, but if it doesn't, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, I don't know. I can't read the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could just before the break just look at one or two examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps -- if the witness for the moment keeps his own note -- well, perhaps you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. This is helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I might not understand the language, but I can make do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, it's helpful. Okay, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 1D5358, page 67 of the B/C/S; and next to it, 65 ter 1D06026, page 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps to assist the witness in his recollection, wouldn't it be fair that you would be given now his notes for a second so that if you ask any questions that he can familiarise himself again with what he wrote about it. And we are at what number? Perhaps a copy could be made of the -- but first, give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to focus your attention to paragraph 2.68 of your report, which is on the left-hand side of the screen; and then in General Radinovic's 2002 Galic report, if we could focus on paragraphs 37 and 38 at the bottom page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This paragraph of your report relates to how command and control functioned in the VRS. First of all, can you confirm that the paragraph of your report, number 2.68, does not contain any citations?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, it does not. And it's 70 per cent paraphrased from paragraphs 37 and 38 of the report of Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I noted that you said it was 70 per cent paraphrased in your notes, but could you please look at the text that's sitting in front of you. The fact is that your paragraph is almost identical in language to paragraphs 37 and 38 of Mr. Radinovic's report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see the first -- paragraph 37 corresponds to the first sentence of your report. Could you continue in paragraph 38, starting with the second sentence in paragraph 2.68 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So General Radinovic's report is almost identical to yours in text up to the words that we see towards the end of paragraph 38 that say "nivo i komandovanja"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the words "nivo i komandovanja," halfway through the third sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I note that appears twice in the paragraph. I don't know if counsel was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. I was speaking from the -- thank you very much. I was speaking from the reference to it, the second line from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The right side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The right side of the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's almost identical to the text of your paragraph, correct, up until that point, paragraphs 37 and 38?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there is a continuation in my text, the last sentence which summarises the previous vision of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's a bit confusing to me because I see your paragraph ends with the same phrase; and then in General Radinovic's report, he continues on with the sentence at the very last line of the page "jedini ozbiljni problem." You're referring to General Radinovic' report, not your own; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the difference in relation to these two paragraphs, so it's 80 per cent identical. The rest of the text is completely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue talking about 70 or 80 per cent, we should clearly define 80 per cent or 70 per cent of what? Your text, what percentage of your text is not taken from the other text? Whether the other text gives something more is a different question. What in your text -- 268, paragraph 268, what percentage of that text is taken from the Radinovic report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 100 per cent identical in this part from 37 and 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we moved from 70 to 80 to now 100. We should always be very carefully if you say for most of them that percentage is taken. If you actually are telling us: By leaving out some portions of the original text, I consider it to be 70 per cent, whereas the 70 per cent you're referring to is for the full 100 per cent identical. Without any reference to the original report, paragraph 268 is for the full 100 per cent identical to a text found in Mr. Radinovic's report. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- no, as a matter of fact, rather not proceed, Mr. Weber, because it's time for a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minute, Witness. Yes, could that be returned to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'll make copies over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's best if you want to continue to work on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if may make use of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could -- I think it would expedite just the topic that we were talking, if we could tender the handwritten list that the witness did that we took into our possession. We're having copies made right now. We will have it translated and then come back to the Chamber and formally tender it into evidence, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then hear from you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I'm not going to spend much more time on the matter we were discussing, but I do have another few questions about it. If one of your students copied from another source and didn't cite or attribute that text to that other source, what -- what would you do as their professor?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially this is an uncited part of the text through the use of about 500 pages of the report of Mr. Radinovic and in question are 35 paragraphs, which is a small fraction of that text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question. I remind you of that, because we do understand from a message from the Victims and Witness Section that you have commitments elsewhere and that you would very much like to conclude your testimony as quickly as possible. Now, it certainly assists in just answering the questions, instead of two or three times not answering the question and then reminded of the question. So if would you please focus. The question was: What would do you with students if they would -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- please answer the question. Mr. Weber will listen because that's what he's supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask him to draw his attention that he should be more careful, but I don't see it's a big problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was just a very simple one. What would you do if one of your students handed in something that didn't cite to another source --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was answered, Mr. Weber. That was when you were perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry, I was distracted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- dealing with other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although Judge Moloto wants to follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say that you wouldn't see it as a very important thing. Am I to understand that you don't consider plagiarism as a very serious breach of professional ethnics by writers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here there can be no question of something like that. I said that it was only 3 per cent of paraphrasing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Stop. Let me stop you. I'm not asking you about here. I'm asking you about your student. You're saying you wouldn't see what your student did as very serious, and I'm saying: Do I understand you to say you don't regard plagiarism as a serious breach of professional ethics in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Plagiarism is taking over the greatest part of the text, not individual paragraphs or sentences; and plagiarism is quite clearly defined in scientific work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer my question. Do you regard plagiarism as a serious misconduct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's not plagiarism. This is not plagiarism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... saying this is plagiarism. I'm just asking the question. Thank you so much. You have answered me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, since you rely on General Radinovic's analysis and many of the same documents, I would like to show you part of his testimony in the Karadzic case and then I'll ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33481, page 7. If we could focus on line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At line 14 of transcript page 41447 in the Karadzic case, General Radinovic was asked: "Q. By working on this case, you learned that -- what the six strategic goals were, and they were actually pursued by the Bosnian Serb leadership and also by General Mladic as commander of the VRS Main Staff. They all shared -- shared these six goals; right? "A. Well, I can suppose they were, but I wasn't involved in that, so I don't know. I don't know that first-hand. I learned about it later. "Q. But by studying the documents you learned that, that they were all pursuing these goals? "A. Yes." First, do you accept that General Radinovic's analysis of the documents is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: By studying the documents for this case, you agree that the Bosnian Serb leadership and General Mladic as commander of the VRS Main Staff all pursued the six strategic objectives; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object that now we're getting a different word than is in the transcript. Strategic goals were mentioned and now we're talking about strategic objectives. If we're talking about something, we need to be very specific about it and maybe even make sure that the witness is talking about the same thing that we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I phrased my question fine, and so I'm asking it -- that's how I'd like to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then you're free to ask the question as you wish. You are aware now of what Mr. Ivetic said. Could the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now quickly when this part of the text is so quickly translated, I said the correlation is correct, but I cannot say yes or no before making a comparative analysis of the text of the translation. And as to what I heard, I think the analysis is correct, the analysis of the interdependence, the correlation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You personally participated in operations that furthered the strategic objectives during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which objectives specifically you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But you participated in Operation Lukavac 93; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Operation Lukavac 93 was in furtherance of the six objectives; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no six objectives. Lukavac 39 was a classical military operation to liberate a previously captured area, and you cannot link it to these six goals, six objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are translated to have said the six objectives or the six goals; that means for you it's the same. I ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is no difference in our language, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that. We received information from the interpreters about there being no difference in language, in your language. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter -- or Exhibit P02508, page 38 of the English and page 41 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, earlier you said: "I don't know which objectives specifically you mean," when reference was made to the six strategic objectives. You are familiar with the strategic objectives, six in number, as they were published; and did you understand it a reference to those six strategic objectives or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean there is no direct relation to the six strategic objectives. This operation was a classical military one and it is not linked to all the objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you said. But earlier you said: I don't know what objective -- which objective specifically you mean to -- in response a question by Mr. Weber. But you are familiar with the six strategic objectives as adopted and published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a portion of General Mladic's speech at the 34th Assembly of Republika Srpska, and I'd like to direct your attention to the centre of the page before you concerning his discussion of Operation Lukovac 93. General Mladic states: "Further, Mr. President, it would be the biggest mistake and catastrophe if we do not impose our own will regarding these maps and if do not exit to the sea. Please, the operation is Lukavac 93. I have deliberately named it as such because at Treskavica there is a geographic point named Lukavac from which the sea can be seen." The fact is, is that Operation Lukavac 93 was even named in furtherance or related to one of the six strategic objectives, gaining access to the sea; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This states a wish, a desire; however, the operation itself does not contain the elements that are directly linked to that goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm done with the document, unless Your Honours had any other questions on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, the first of these strategic objectives was the separation from the other two national communities. What documents did you reference in your report that show the VRS pursued this objective, if you could refer us to any?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Separation between the two or, rather, all the three ethnic communities was a process that went on the whole time of the war and is linked essentially to all the command documents of all the three armies. Separation between armies meant, in that civil war, also separation between the peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that all of the VRS command documents pursued the first strategic objective of separation from the other national communities; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying. I said precisely that it refers to all the three armies and all the three ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any documents that you reviewed in your report that come to mind - VRS documents - that clearly indicate to you that the VRS was pursuing the first strategic objective, the separation of the national communities?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done, in fact, even before the Army of Republika Srpska was established. And when I spoke about the Sarajevo theatre of war, during the defence the initial armed formations of the armed people affected the separation between the peoples; and the armies, when they were arrived, when they were established, already found that situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll come back to this topic. Did you rely on General Radinovic's material because you agreed with his opinions and views?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known General Radinovic a long time, more than 30 years. He used to be my superior and an example I tried to follow. On many things we agree and we exchanged views and findings in our expert reports, and we lent each other assistance to the extent possible; and I believe that in many things we do agree, but there are also issues where we do not agree completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's explore this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33435a.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Coming up will be a speech by General Radinovic at a rally for Vojislav Seselj in Belgrade. This speech was published in one of Mr. Seselj's books in 2005. Directing your attention to the second paragraph of the speech where General Radinovic states: "Why was he arrested in the first place? Well, simply because Seselj is a metaphor for Serb patriotism and the Serb identity." Do you agree with General Radinovic that Seselj is a metaphor for Serb patriotism and the Serb identity?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know about this statement of his or about this rally. Personally I do not think in exactly the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You are aware that Vojislav Seselj advocated for the creation of a Greater Serbia, connecting parts of the Republics of Serbia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about such statements and such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Later in the speech General Radinovic states: "I would like -- I would just like to underline a few of my professional -- personal impressions on The Hague, i.e., The Hague Tribunal, where I was misfortunate enough to have had occasion to be several times, trying to testify in the defence of Serbian generals. So further to what I believe most deeply and what I have learned, The Hague Tribunal is a powerful means of the West's extended aggression against our country." Do you share these views with General Radinovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a complete position on that, but having attended this part of the trial so far, I can see that there is a pretty one-sided views of many matters. In scientific research and work, when one comes to any judgement about events during armed conflict without access to documents or being aware of the positions of the other side, it is impossible to get to the truth. In these entire proceedings so far, what is being done is mostly an analysis of documents and actions of only one side, which points to a conclusion that we cannot talk about objective findings regarding specific events. And then from that aspect, the The Hague and The Hague Tribunal have been recognised among the Serbian people as an instrument whose goal is not to get to the ultimate truth but to confirm an already created media image of the war in the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I would like to ask you: Can you explain what you mean when you say, and I quote: "But having attended this part of the trial so as far ...," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I specifically meant was that as soon as you refer to or try to clarify a specific time-frame of an event, this is prevented, it's interrupted. A specific example: Yesterday when we were speaking about Podvelezje, I tried to provide a couple of assertions regarding the status of inter-ethnic relations at the beginning of the civil war in that area during that period and I was not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hear what you are saying. Later in your previous answer, you said: "In these entire proceedings so far, what is being done is mostly an analysis of documents an actions of only one side." Again, what do you mean by "these entire proceedings so far"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I mean is my participation so far, my testimony here so far, and that documents, orders, directives, and actions are not being taken into consideration at the same time of the other party to the conflict. Without such an approach in scientific research, I am saying it is impossible to view all of the dimensions of an event or get to the truth. I'm talking about the main principles, scientific research principle, when one is considering conflicts, wars, crisis, and so on because all of these crisis, armed conflicts, wars, are something that occurs from two sides at least and you cannot just look at one side in order to reach a decision. We're talking about the political and military dimension as well when we're considering this. This is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand your position, but it is not correct. It's not your task to criticise the Chamber. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have one other question since you are saying this. Was there anything you couldn't write in your report to bring to our attention so that we could consider it? Was there any limitation? Did you experience any limitation in what you would put in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, I apologise. I was not criticizing the work of the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... well, Witness, we'll read what you said and then we'll consider whether this is criticism or not, but I do understand that you did not intend to do it. But could you please answer my question? You said that it was a problem that it was all one-sided. Now, my question to you is: Was there any limitation in presenting your views on the matter in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have limitations, and I noted those right at the very beginning, and that is the number of documents and their contents that referred to the operations of the Croatian army, the HVO, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I was indirectly trying to get to them through monographs, books, studies, and the like that were published in those countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who imposed those limitations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The actual situation. I could not get those documents. I couldn't receive orders, plans for actions of the B and H army and the Croatian army covering this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you asked the Defence to seek the assistance of the Chamber to get access to materials that you were missing, that were missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, several times in conversations with the Defence lawyers, I did note the problem of sources relating to combat documents and plans of the other armies that were party to the civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you say the Tribunal prohibited access to those materials? Because you said that it's the Tribunal who is one-sidedly dealing with the matter. So I'm just -- I'm taking your observation seriously and I want to hear from you in what way this Tribunal, in one way, was an obstacle to get to the sources you thought you would need to write your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in what manner, but I was not able to get those sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there are two different questions. First, whether you had access to the sources; and second, whether this Tribunal contributed specifically in not having access. These are two -- what did you intend to say, that you didn't have access; or that the Tribunal was more or less prohibiting or assisting in you not having access to it? I just would like to know what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not get the documents through the Defence. I don't know what their relationship is vis-à-vis the Court, whether they were able to do so or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say, I didn't have access. I asked for it to the Defence, but whether the Tribunal did what it should have do -- should do, that is, to facilitate the Defence in getting access to that, that you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That part I don't know, but I just mentioned the example yesterday about the issue regarding stating information about a specific event, but it was insisted that answers be given on specific items in the order, specifically the order of the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand what you mean. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I rose for a different point so I'm not actually addressing this that you have been -- in relation to. I just wanted to make clear that when the witness was interrupted in terms of explaining that he was not criticising the Chamber, I want to make it clear that he was, at both instances, answering a question posed by Mr. Weber and answering a question posed by Judge Fluegge. So what the witness was doing was answering the questions that were posed to him, which I believe we will all agree is the task of a witness here, to answer questions posed to them. So I want to make sure that in translation there wasn't any kind of inference that the witness is not to answer questions that he's been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one blames the witness for answering the question, and he sometimes does answer questions. But to say that if there's a duty to answer a question, that doesn't mean that there's no implicit criticism in the answer and the witness can be asked about such criticism. And of course, at the end of this short line of questioning, Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber of course would very much like to know, in view of the answers of the witness, where its assistance was sought to get access to certain documents and where we said: Well, we're not going to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, my memory is a bit faulty because it's been about three and a half years, but we did ask for access to other cases, including cases against Bosnian Muslim and Croatian defendants. And I believe that some of those motions for access to documents from other cases were denied. I could be wrong because I'm only going off of memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, it's important -- by this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This Chamber has been the only Chamber seized of this case since the beginning of my involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. If we -- if we failed to do what we're supposed to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, I could be wrong. I'm only working off a faint memory that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please refresh your memory in the coming days and let us know by Monday because -- of course this Chamber is trying to do its job as seriously as we can. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 33435a into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P7672, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33436 page 1 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up is the -- is a 22 April 1994 Nin interview of General Radinovic. Directing your attention to the question in the centre column, which is part of a discussion on the importance of Gorazde, it states: "You're talking about the significance it has for the Muslims. And for the Serbs?" General Radinovic answers: "What is important for us is that the Muslims do not achieve this goal, that is, that the so-called green transversal be severed. It is important to us that the SR Yugoslavia border towards the former BiH be as secure as possible, and it will be more secure if this section of the border is in possession of the, I hope, new Serb state." The new Serb state that General Radinovic is speaking about in 1994 would connect parts of Serbia, the RSK, and the Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under that name, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page, in the upper portion of the far right column in front of you, General Radinovic is asked about whether one can find fault with whether some cities were not predominantly -- were not predominantly Serb before the war, mentioning Brcko and Zvornik. He answers: "The matter at hand is that it has to be acknowledged that a state cannot continue to exist if it has no essential prerequisites and one of them is the territorial connectedness of the entities populated by an ethnic majority. In the final demarcation to, an injustice will have certainly been done to different localities but this can be balanced out through a certain exchange of territories." We'll go step by step here. First, the Serb political and military leadership sought a territorial connected state consisting of areas where Serbs would be in an ethnic majority; that's what happened during the war, right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but that applies to Muslims, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the areas where the Serbs were not a majority before the war, this would result in an injustice to those living in part -- those living in parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning when I was commenting on the civil war in Bosnia, yes, that led to the transfer of people from one area to another. I don't want to waste time by mentioning figures, but -- for example, after the war, approximately 120.000 Serbs from Sarajevo left that city. They went to live in other areas, to Podrinje, to Semberija, to Posavina. Many of them emigrated to Western countries, including Australia, Canada, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, it resulted in an injustice to people in a whole lot of other municipalities too, like Brcko and Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many mixed communities, yes, but this applies to all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 33436 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honours. The part that has been presented to the witness he has answered. The Prosecution's cross-examination that they asked for this witness was on his expert report, his expert opinions. This document has nothing to do with the expert report, nor the expert opinions of this witness. Therefore, they cannot bring in an interview with somebody -- if they want to bring an interview of somebody, they need to bring a witness to authenticate the interview, they need to bring a witness to comply with the Rules for statements taken outside of court that they want to rely upon. So in this sense, since I think we've endeavoured enough of this questioning by Mr. Weber that not relate to the expertise of this witness -- we have yet to even start talking about the expertise of this witness and his conclusions -- and here we are already into the second or third hour. When are we going to get to the expertise of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak aloud; he should stick to that. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am really not going to respond to most of what Ivetic -- Mr. Ivetic just said. Put simply, he has heavily relied on General Radinovic. He's expressed opinions in his report. I think it's perfectly fair game to put to this witness views that General Radinovic held during the war; that's what I've done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. At the same time, Mr. Weber, you're encouraged to avoid that we finally deal with Mr. Radinovic only -- irrespective of how much the witness relied on it and rather go to the report primarily. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. Could the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I think it was in the -- the document was tendered. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33436 receives Exhibit Number P7673, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 06009, page 22 of the B/C/S and page 20 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 21 January 1993 session of the council for co-ordinating state policy. Present at the session are a number of individuals, including General Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Slobodan Milosevic, among others. At the bottom of this page, we see that Radovan Karadzic is speaking. He says: "There was 50/50 of us in Zvornik. The number of inhabitants of Zvornik is now the same, approximately 50.000, and they are all Serbs. More than 24.000 Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia have arrived and stopped in Zvornik." This is an example of how municipalities, like Zvornik, were ethnically redistributed during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, in comparison with other areas, the same way that the ethnic structure was changed in Mostar when we're looking at Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please focus your answer. Whether the same thing happened elsewhere in the opposite way is certainly a matter which may be relevant, then you'll be asked about it by the Defence or later by Mr. Weber, but could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just commenting on the question in the way that I am viewing it right now. It's simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you're not invited to comment on the question. You're invited to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems as if what is being asked of me is to say, yes. When there is a deliberate way of putting a question to me, it seems that I'm expected to say yes. I cannot respond to a question in that manner. If these are yes-and-no questions, then I cannot answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, can you say no, you can say yes, you can say -- but what you're supposed to do is to stick to the issue which is part of the question, and the issue was about Zvornik and not about what happened elsewhere. If that's relevant, questions will be put, for example, by the Defence. And this perhaps also explains perhaps some misunderstanding of what a trial, that is this one, how it is conducted. That is one party asks you questions, you're supposed to answer those questions; another party has introduced a 500-page report in which you may have expressed whatever you thought relevant, and then additional questions can be put to you by the Defence. That's how it works. Could you pleas answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, the question was: Is this an example -- is Zvornik an example of what is going on in other municipalities. Without talking about other municipalities, the witness cannot answer the question. So I'm confused as an attorney as to what is going on here, because the question asked in relation to other municipalities is Zvornik an example? The witness started answering it and he was not allowed to answer, so I really am concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, what concerns you here is incomprehensible to me. The question is: Is this an example of what happened during the war? You can answer yes or no, and if you want to add other examples that support this example, it's up to you to do so; or, if not, you in re-examination can ask about other examples to elaborate on that. There is no need when you are asked about an example to then start giving a litany of other examples which are not being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that question that you posed was asked to the witness, I would agree with you; but that's not the question that Mr. Weber posed. The question Mr. Weber posed introduced other municipalities, and therefore the witness - in my opinion - is quite right to answer in the way he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, let me just try. Mr. Weber asked: This is an example of how municipalities, like Zvornik, were ethnically redistributed during the war; correct? Now the witness can say either this is an example or it is not an example. He thinks that he should say yes; he can say no as well. And then Mr. Weber may have follow-up questions to find out why this witness - and that's apparently what he wishes to do - why the witness is concerned about the way in which the question was phrased. So if you think it's not an example, Witness, you just say no, and then Mr. Weber will put further questions or Mr. Ivetic will later put further questions to you. There's no way that are you expected to say yes. You can say no if you think it's not an example. Therefore, carefully listen to the question. Don't comment - as the witness said he did - on the question, and listen to the next question put to you by Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You could also say you don't know, if you don't know the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, what we see here is an example of how municipalities, specifically referring to this example with Zvornik, were ethnically redistributed during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for all three warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 65 of the B/C/S and page 55 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During this meeting there's much discussion and continued discussion of maps. On this page, General Mladic is speaking and he states: "[As read] They are, in every way, going to try to negate the state of facts by the principle of non-recognition of territories conquered by force, which is not the case in the maps, not even as regards this -- not event as regards this principle."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should repeat the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "They are, in every way, going to try to negate the state of facts by the principle of non-recognition of territories conquered by force, which is not the case in the maps, not even as regards this principle." By January 1993, the VRS had conquered territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina by force; you're aware of that, right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three armies conquered by force during the civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The VRS did that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if the witness says all three parties, then the VRS is included. There's no need to -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The paragraph ends with the statement: "They don't want to give the same to us." In the context of this paragraph, General Mladic is complaining that the maps being negotiated do not reflect the areas that the VRS conquered; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither see the map nor do I know which areas are being discussed, so I cannot draw a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to come back to this document a little bit later in my examination and I'm going to move on to another topic, but if this is an okay time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for the break. But before we take that break, Witness, I'd like to add something to an earlier conversation that was conducted in this courtroom. The question was about whether this is an example of that. Now apparently, after thinking it over, it may have been unclear and Mr. Weber may not have been very clear on it being an example of what. Apparently you understood the question - although that was certainly not explicit - that this is an example of what happened to municipalities where then a Serb majority came in, or whether this was an example of something that happened in all municipalities where one ethnicity became the majority after certain events, and that would then be for the whole of the countries. Now, Mr. Weber has not been very explicit in that respect in his question. So apart from a "yes" or a "no" or "I don't know," if the question is unclear to you, you may ask for clarification of that question. At the same time, apparently you interpreted the question in a certain way, that is, that Mr. Weber was asking about this was an example of what happened to non-Serb majority municipalities that then became a Serb majority. That's how you interpreted it. The question wasn't clear in that respect. You considered it important to broaden it and to make it example of perhaps of what happened in all municipalities. Now, if you would have asked: Mr. Weber, do you mean it to be an example of what happened in municipalities where finally there was a Serb majority at the end, or did you ask me about what happened in all municipalities, irrespective of what ethnicity finally ended up to the majority? That would have been a fair request for clarification. But that's different from commenting on a question as you understood it. You could have asked for clarification. We take a break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to -- yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have used the break to refresh my recollection as to a decision by this Trial Chamber of 7 September 2012, where this Trial Chamber in a written decision denied the Defence access to confidential documents from the case of Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic, who was commander of the ABH army; the case of Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Kubura, also a member of the ABiH; to the case of Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic, commander-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down. It's impossible to follow for the transcriber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The case of Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic, who was commander-in-chief of the ABiH, and for which we were also denied access; to the case of Prosecutor versus Zdravko Mucic et al., which was in relation to Celebici camp in Konjic municipality; and also the case of Prosecutor versus Naser Oric, who was commander of the 28th Division in the Srebrenica area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all in that that one decision, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then we'll re- visit that decision and see what the reasons were, whether it was unwillingness to assist the Defence or whether there were any other reasons which led us to those decisions. We'll have a have look at it. Thank you for informing us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of your report, this is in the introduction, you state: "It is true that all the three peoples in BH were exposed to ethnic cleansing and crimes." Just for clarity, the three peoples that you are referring to are the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Croats, and the Bosnian Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, and they're not only Bosnian. This adjective, Bosnian, does not feature in practice among the people, it's not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You say it does not feature in practice among the people. What people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this attribute, Bosnian, because Bosnia-Herzegovina was established as a socialist republic in the former SFRY and it has predominantly the Bosnian and the Herzegovinian parts. When you say "Bosnian," it excludes Herzegovina. That's why we use the terms Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, later called Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the paragraph, you describe how Serbs were subjected to ethnic cleansing. How were the Muslims ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one paragraph, it can be expressed as follows. From the beginning of the civil war, by establishing front lines between paramilitary formations and later with the establishment of the armies, with the movement of armies, people were moved from one territory to another, controlled by their own army. So they were moved in the same way as Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You consider this to be ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's arguable whether it was by ethnic cleansing, but you can say that a division among the peoples occurred. Some people left their territory in the initial period under the pressure of paramilitaries, but generally you can apply that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: They never left under pressure from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left from the pressure of all the three armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What crimes were committed against the Muslims? And if could you be specific as possible as to where the crimes occurred and when they happened.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my first association is the mass crime in Srebrenica, and that stands as a symbol of the mass crime in Srebrenica, although there are crimes less known and less covered by the media that were committed in the course of the civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. What lesser-known crimes were committed against Muslims? And if you could again be as specific as possible.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm using the term "lesser" under quotation marks. Every crime is a crime. I am speaking only in terms of the number of victims, and again, I don't want to play even with the number of victims. But there were crimes in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. I specifically couldn't remember an event now, but when we talk about losses in the Sarajevo battle-field, if around five and a half thousand Muslim soldiers are killed and 2.500 Serb soldiers get killed, then in all this killing crimes are perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You aware that thousands of civilians were killed inside the inner ring of Sarajevo during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I cited various sources, and different numbers are encountered as to the suffering of civilians, both Serbs and Muslims in Sarajevo. I know that the commander of the 1st Corps of the BH army at the end of the war spoke about the losses in his corps, the number of those killed and wounded, seriously or less seriously; but I remember the figure of 10.400 total of civilians killed in Sarajevo, both Muslims and Serbs. If necessary, I can say something about the structure Mr. Mehanowski [phoen] made an analysis of the losses in the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll come back and discuss Sarajevo, in particular. Can you tell us now specifically as possible what crimes were committed against Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the Croats? I know in Central Bosnia, in the area of Lasva, Zenica, Travnik, around Kiseljak, and towards Mostar, from Jablanica in the direction of Mostar, I don't know specific place names, but I know that in the period when the HVO and the BH army were in conflict, significant crimes against the civilian population and property occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any crimes committed by the VRS against the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the Croatian population? I don't know of any mass crimes. I cannot remember any mass crimes, only individual ones. At the time of an intensive conflict between the Croats and Muslims, the Serbian side provided logistics and helped rescue the Croatian population from Central Bosnia and transferred them across their territory up to western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a single document that you reference in your report which indicates any member of the VRS committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A great number of reports refer to units on lower tactical level and paramilitary formations that committed crimes, and this report does not deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You make reference to the six strategic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ask you: I understood the question to be - but please correct me when I am wrong - whether you referenced any document in which the commission of a crime by VRS members is mentioned. Your answer was: "A great number of reports refer to units on lower tactical level and paramilitary formations that committed crimes." Now, that's not exactly the same, whether you are referring to documents dealing with crimes committed or that you have referenced documents referring to units, where you do not deny that they had committed crimes. Therefore, I don't know to what extent your answer is really an answer to the question: Have you referred to documents which specifically deal with crimes committed by members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for instance, the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, but I was mainly concerned about whether the understanding of the question and the answer was linking to the question. But if you give that example, that would most certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] For example, the order of the Chief of Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, where it is noted that some of the men of their own accord opened fire without receiving any orders and it is defined which measures should be taken in future, if it happens again, against such individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that order is referenced in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, was that -- you will understand that I have no recollection. Was that because they have violated discipline, or was it that they had committed crimes against the opposite party? Because, again, that's not the same, because opening fire without instructions does not necessarily mean that you commit a crime. You may violate -- Could you tell us whether it's described in that document as a crime committed against, I take it, the other party, either civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not stated explicitly, but it can be concluded - it can be inferred - that if somebody opened fire of their own accord without orders, that they could have committed a crime, such as killing an innocent person or persons in that area. It's not explicitly linked, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an example where a document is referred to where it's clearly stated that VRS soldiers committed a crime, but you say could have been. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on your example, what's the date of that document? And if you can, give me -- I presume it's in the Sarajevo part of your report. Who was it from, if could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Sarajevo chapter the year is 1994 - I cannot remember the date - but it's in the footnote, both the reference to the document and the signatory is mentioned. I know he's the Chief of Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In 1994 that would be Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the commander. I said Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is this the beginning half of 1994; and, if so, would that be Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not the first half. It's the second half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just help us out tomorrow morning with a reference is to that document, it would be appreciated, if you wouldn't mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just -- who was the Chief of Staff at that time of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know only the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You make reference to the six strategic goals of the RS in paragraph 4.206 of your report, along with their acceptance at the 16th Assembly Session on 12 May 1992. I'd like to go through some documents with you now for the rest of the day and ask you some questions about how these were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P07086.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 26 May 1992 Birac Brigade order. Item 6 of the order says: "Move women and children out of the Muslim villages to Kalesija and Gracanica, whereas the men are to be taken away to collection centres." This order shows the army implemented the first objective by moving non-Serbs from villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this: You see in the signature, it is a brigade commander, a major. It's two months into the war. It's the area of Podrinje where the Muslim and Serb villages were intermixed, and it's an act of moving people to areas under the control of their army. It says here "move." I don't see the dimension of mistreatment anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You agree it's the Serb forces, the VRS, that is doing this; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. Both armies did that, the BH army and the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P7408.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We are now going to discuss a sequence of documents. First, this is operational order number 1 from SRK Commander Stanislav Galic dated 14 September 1992. This order was issued shortly after General Galic became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to these elements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under section 4.6, related to the tasks of the brigades, General Galic orders the Rogatica Brigade to take the sector of Mount Gosina in co-ordination with the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. You were aware that Mount Gosina is located to the south of the village of Nevosoci which is located in the municipality of Sokolac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33447.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 10 September 1992 SRK command regular combat report from General Galic to the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could go to item 3 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The English version that I have goes from item 2 to 4, so I'm not quite sure where item 3 would be exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might have gone to the incorrect document. I'll come back to it first thing in the morning once I check the upload.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P6641 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 20 September 1992 2nd Romanija Brigade attack order from Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page, we see that Colonel Krstic, at the time, orders the 1st and 5th Battalions to carry out an attack along the Olovo axis - do you see that? - among other areas.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is almost illegible. I cannot make it out. Half of the words cannot be read.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Court Officer could please assist and enlarge points 5 and 6 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is that better, sir?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little better, but there's certainly 40 per cent of the text I can't read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there specific portions, because apparently this text is translated and therefore deciphered first. If there are any specific portions you think you couldn't read, then we could ask Mr. Weber to slowly read the English translation so as to make you familiar with what the original is supposed to say. And, I take it, Mr. Ivetic, that you'll keep a close eye on it, that it corresponds with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I look in the -- under item 5 that the 1st mtb shall carry out the attack from the -- and it's a little bit unlegible [sic] but, Grah, a specific trigger point, and then, legible, is Krusevo Biostica river line, along the Donje Krusevo-Prgosevo-Olovo-Olog access. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you able to see under -- in the next section, number 6, that the 5th mtb is to carry out an attack using the main forces and as part of the line that they're supposed to operate on, it includes Olovo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P3822.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 22 September 1992, 2nd Romanija Brigade combat report from Colonel Krstic to the VRS Main Staff and SRK command. Focussing on item 1b, as in boy, the report states: "Units from our brigade carried out activities yesterday in the area of Mount Gosina in a joint operation with the Rogatica" -- the word "brigade," I see, is actually missing from the translation but in the original "with the aim to reach the Praca valley. Units of the 1st and 5th mtb also engaged in activities in the direction of Olovo with the aim to establish conditions to move into attack and take control of Olovo and the Nisici-Olovo-Han Pijesak road. During the day, the village of Nevosoci was ciscenje in Glasinacko Polje." This report indicates that General Galic's and Colonel Krstic's orders that we saw previously were carried out; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this report, you can only see the concept. What the effects are, we cannot see. Unfortunately, this concept is pejorative. Cleansing, "ciscenje," and the connotation is pejorative. Tell me what you understand this term to mean, "ciscenje"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll come to that term in a second but what I'm asking you actually is that we looked at General Galic's order and then following on from that, Colonel Krstic's order, and you'd agree those orders were carried out by the 2nd Romanija Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this report ties in with the previous order. At least the time sequence, the dates, seem to indicate so. Although perhaps not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've commented already, and we see as part of these operations the 2nd Romanija Brigade reports that it ciscenje'd the village of Nevosoci on 22nd September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P4162 for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to go through two more documents with you on this before the end of the day. This is an Associated Press article about 41 Muslims being buried in Bosnia. In the third paragraph, it states: "Nevosoci died on September 22, 1992, when Serb units assembled the small farming population in front of the mosque. Forty-five males were marched away. Damir Ocuz, at 14, was the youngest. Edhem Karic was 85. Everyone else fled." This article is consistent with other evidence that the Prosecution has led in this case, including, P717, P727 and, lastly, P3170, which reflects that two mentioned people, and others, including Damir Ocuz and Edhem Karic, were murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P17 [sic] for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We're just look to look at this document and then I'll try and ask my follow-up questions for the day. P719; my apologies. This is a 26 September 1992 approval from Colonel Krstic. It certifies that a conscript of the 2nd Romanija Brigade can transport a bunch of furniture and appliances from Nevosoci to Sokolac. It also indicates that the conscript has chosen a house in Nevosoci for future living. So based on the last two documents that we looked at, the fact is, is that activities that ciscenje the village of Nevosoci resulted in Muslims being removed and members of the VRS occupying their houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the direct connection to members of the VRS. It's about one of the residents who came to live in that house, somebody who also had left his home. It's not a soldiers who's moving in but a family that had left another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I see your focussing on the immediate document that is before you. The reason I went through a whole sequence of them was to eventually ask you that question. So, not just exclusively this document but the series of documents we looked at, show that, in fact, operations or activities to ciscenje the village resulted in Muslims being removed and Serbs moving into their houses; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a one-sided conclusion, and I don't think it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I actually see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one clarifying point before we break off. Sir, you said you can't see the direct connection to members of the VRS within this document. This document gives approval to Dragomir Bozic from the 2nd RM BTBR. Isn't that a VRS unit? And then it says in the second paragraph: "The above mentioned items will be transferred until final moving into a house in Nevosoci which the above-named has chosen for future living." Now "the above-named" is Dragomir Bozic, who comes from a battalion of the VRS. Is it not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's he and his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not just a resident. It is this person, this resident who is a soldier of the VRS. Now, your answer was you don't see direct connection to members of the VRS. Now he is a member of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he is with his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll adjourn for the day. Chamber is aware, and the parties are aware as well, I think, that you'd like to conclude your testimony tomorrow. I don't know whether that's possible or not. If that requires any further actions, then please inform VWS. And I'm looking at both parties to see whether it's feasible. Mr. Weber, you say it's not -- at least that's what I understand from your nodding no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time have you used until now and what time did you announce?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will check and give a more precise identification in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because a simple no is not binding on the Chamber as you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. I do anticipate that we'll probably be through tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see. We'll further -- well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've used two hours and 30 minutes until now, I do understand. Then, Witness, I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate to anyone about your testimony, whether given already or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, your reference to the decision of - what was it? - the 2012 decision in which the Chamber denied access to, you are referring to the decision in which, I think, for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 28 cases access was granted and that for five cases where there was no geographic overlap or no temporary [sic] overlap, and, therefore, that the forensic purpose was insufficiently demonstrated in the view of the Chamber, that that's the decision you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The five decisions on cases as to Muslim commanders of the ABiH in Sarajevo and in Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was temporary and geographic overlap. And, please, do you remember whether you sought certification to appeal that decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this distance from that decision any answer I give would not be reliable since I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We'll -- and then another question is: Did you -- because this witness specifically said something about that he wished to have access to certain documents. Did you ever follow that up by asking for specific documentation where there was an overlap so as to seek the assistance of the Chamber in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I only met with the witness when he came here in The Hague, so the discussions with him and I were two days before he started testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please check whether the witness has had conversations with members of the Mladic Defence team and whether there ever was a request which were then followed up in court so that we could have assisted, or perhaps would have denied assistance, in getting access to those documents specifically for this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would be surprised if there were, since I think I would be aware of anything that was brought into the courtroom -- well, I certainly don't recall having personally made such a request to the Chamber. I could say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, where the -- I may have pronounced not very precisely, I talked about the temporarily and geographic overlap and not about the temporary overlap but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Temporal, I think, is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Temporal. Yes. Overlap in terms of time and geography so that avoids any further problem. With the apologies for the late adjournment, we'll resume tomorrow, 19th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
